subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: During the link reaction and Krebs cycle, how many molecules of carbon dioxide are released in total per single glucose molecule?
questions.explain: Two CO2 come from the two link reactions and four from the two Krebs turns, giving four overall here.

questions.q: An irreversible inhibitor such as a heavy metal ion binding to a sulfhydryl group at the active site would be classified by its mechanism as broadly:
options: an inhibitor that permanently alters the enzyme so activity is not restored by adding substrate
a competitive inhibitor that can be reversed by adding substrate
questions.explain: Irreversible inhibitors bind so strongly (often covalently) that activity cannot be restored simply by increasing substrate concentration.

questions.q: When a fully turgid plant cell has its pressure potential exactly balancing its solute potential, its water potential is zero, meaning:
options: there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell when surrounded by pure water
questions.explain: At full turgor the inward pressure potential equals the solute potential in magnitude, giving Psi = 0, so no net water movement occurs with pure water outside.

questions.q: In contrast, increasing the concentration of a NON-COMPETITIVE inhibitor would:
options: reduce Vmax because raising substrate cannot displace the inhibitor
increase the enzyme's affinity for substrate
questions.explain: Because non-competitive inhibitors do not compete for the active site, additional substrate cannot reverse their effect, so Vmax is reduced.

questions.q: Which factor would increase the permeability of a cell membrane?
options: An increase in temperature, increasing phospholipid movement and creating gaps
A decrease in temperature, increasing phospholipid order
questions.explain: Higher temperatures increase phospholipid kinetic energy and fluidity, and can denature membrane proteins, increasing permeability.

questions.q: Why do lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates when respired?
options: They contain more carbon-hydrogen bonds to be oxidised, releasing more reduced coenzymes
questions.explain: Lipids are highly reduced with many C-H bonds, so their oxidation yields more reduced NAD and FAD and thus more ATP.

questions.q: Which molecule is phosphorylated using ATP at the start of glycolysis, before the sugar is split?
questions.explain: Glucose is first phosphorylated to glucose phosphate, making it more reactive before it is split into two triose phosphates.

questions.q: An advantage of using immobilised enzymes in industrial processes is that:
options: they react faster than free enzymes in all cases
the enzyme can be recovered and reused, and does not contaminate the product
they have a lower optimum temperature
questions.explain: Immobilising enzymes on an inert support allows easy recovery, reuse and a product free of enzyme contamination, often with greater thermal stability.

questions.q: What is the NET yield of ATP from one molecule of glucose during glycolysis alone?
questions.explain: Four ATP are produced but two are invested in the early phosphorylation steps, giving a net gain of two ATP.

questions.q: A low Km value for an enzyme indicates that the enzyme:
options: has a low affinity for its substrate
reaches half its maximum rate at a low substrate concentration, indicating high affinity
questions.explain: If half-maximal rate is reached at low substrate concentration, the enzyme binds substrate readily, so a low Km means high affinity.

questions.q: In glycolysis, the six-carbon hexose bisphosphate is split to form two molecules of which three-carbon compound?
questions.explain: Hexose bisphosphate is lysed into two molecules of triose phosphate, each of which is then oxidised to pyruvate.

questions.q: In mammalian muscle during anaerobic respiration, what is the key role of reducing pyruvate to lactate?
options: To produce carbon dioxide for gas exchange
To regenerate NAD so glycolysis can continue
To synthesise acetyl CoA for the Krebs cycle
questions.explain: Reducing pyruvate oxidises reduced NAD back to NAD, allowing glycolysis and its ATP yield to continue without oxygen.

questions.q: Above the optimum temperature, enzyme activity falls because:
options: substrate molecules move too slowly to collide
the activation energy decreases too far
hydrogen and ionic bonds break, changing the tertiary structure and active site shape
more enzyme-substrate complexes form than can be processed
questions.explain: Excessive thermal energy breaks bonds holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the active site so the substrate no longer fits.

questions.q: The water potential of pure water at standard temperature and pressure is:
options: equal to the solute potential of the cell
questions.explain: Pure water has the highest water potential, defined as 0 kPa; adding solute makes the water potential more negative.

questions.q: Where in the cell does the link reaction take place?
questions.explain: After pyruvate is actively transported into the mitochondrion, the link reaction occurs in the matrix.

questions.q: The induced-fit model differs from the lock-and-key model in that:
options: the substrate changes shape to fit a rigid active site
the active site changes shape as the substrate binds to fit more closely
the active site is exactly complementary to the substrate before binding
questions.explain: In the induced-fit model the active site moulds around the substrate on binding, straining bonds and stabilising the transition state.

questions.q: Cells specialised for absorption, such as the epithelial cells of the ileum, increase their rate of uptake by having:
options: fewer carrier proteins to reduce competition
microvilli that greatly increase the surface area of the membrane for transport proteins
questions.explain: Microvilli increase the membrane surface area, providing more sites for carrier and co-transport proteins and so faster absorption.

questions.q: Two cells are in contact: cell A has a water potential of -400 kPa and cell B has -750 kPa. Water will move:
options: in both directions equally with no net movement
not at all because the cells are isolated
from cell A to cell B
from cell B to cell A
questions.explain: Water moves from a higher (less negative) water potential to a lower (more negative) one, i.e. from A (-400) to B (-750).

questions.q: At very high temperatures an enzyme loses activity permanently, whereas at very low temperatures activity is merely slowed. This difference exists because:
options: high temperature lowers the activation energy
low temperature breaks bonds in the tertiary structure
high temperature breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds causing irreversible denaturation, while low temperature only reduces kinetic energy
questions.explain: Denaturation at high temperature permanently disrupts the active site, but cold simply reduces molecular movement, which is reversible on warming.

questions.q: Increasing the number of channel and carrier proteins in a membrane would increase the rate of facilitated diffusion only if:
options: there is still a concentration gradient and proteins were previously the limiting factor
the molecules are non-polar and small
the temperature is reduced to zero
questions.explain: More transport proteins raise the rate only when proteins limit it and a gradient remains to drive the movement.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it:
options: uses channel or carrier proteins to move polar/charged molecules down their gradient
only occurs across the nuclear envelope
moves substances against their concentration gradient
questions.explain: Facilitated diffusion is passive but uses transport proteins to allow polar or charged molecules to cross the hydrophobic bilayer, still down the gradient.

questions.q: What is the approximate respiratory quotient (RQ) for the complete aerobic respiration of a carbohydrate such as glucose?
questions.explain: For glucose the volumes of CO2 produced and O2 consumed are equal, giving an RQ of 1.0.

questions.q: Below the optimum temperature, the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction is low mainly because:
options: the active site has changed shape permanently
substrate and enzyme molecules have less kinetic energy, so successful collisions forming complexes are less frequent
questions.explain: At lower temperatures molecules move more slowly, reducing the frequency of effective collisions and the formation of enzyme-substrate complexes.

questions.q: Many enzymes require a cofactor such as a metal ion (e.g. Zn2+ or Cl-) because the cofactor:
options: denatures the enzyme to expose the active site
is a non-protein component needed for the enzyme to function
questions.explain: Cofactors are non-protein helpers required for catalytic activity, sometimes altering the active site shape to allow binding.

questions.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction typically decrease over time when measured as product formed?
options: The activation energy increases over time
Substrate concentration falls as it is converted to product, reducing collision frequency
The enzyme is denatured by the product
questions.explain: As substrate is depleted, fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, so the rate declines until substrate runs out.

questions.q: Some toxins inhibit ATP synthase. What is the most direct effect on a respiring cell?
options: The proton gradient collapses immediately and the chain speeds up
Protons accumulate in the intermembrane space and ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis stops
questions.explain: With the channel blocked, protons cannot flow back through the enzyme, so the gradient builds and ATP production halts.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium across a membrane during diffusion:
options: molecules continue to move in both directions but there is no net movement
molecules move only from low to high concentration
questions.explain: At equilibrium molecules still move randomly both ways, but with equal rates so there is no net change in concentration.

questions.q: A channel protein differs from a carrier protein in facilitated diffusion in that a channel protein:
options: changes shape to move molecules across
forms a hydrophilic pore allowing specific ions to pass without changing shape
questions.explain: Channel proteins provide a water-filled pore for specific ions to diffuse through, whereas carrier proteins change conformation to shuttle molecules across.

questions.q: In aerobic respiration, what is the terminal (final) electron acceptor of the electron transport chain?
questions.explain: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, combining with electrons and protons to form water.

questions.q: A small mammal consumes 10 cm3 of oxygen and produces 8 cm3 of carbon dioxide in the same period. What is its respiratory quotient?
questions.explain: RQ = CO2 produced / O2 consumed = 8 / 10 = 0.8.
